title: What is a portfolio?
subtitle: A collection of investments managed as a single whole
openingQuestion: You have 100 million VND, split equally across 5 stocks in different industries. What is this collection of 5 stocks called?
openingOptions: A portfolio - a set of assets held and managed together as a single unit
explanation: A portfolio is the collection of every investment (stocks, bonds, cash, real estate...) an investor holds, viewed and managed as ONE unified whole - not as separate individual positions. Portfolio thinking is the foundation of all of modern investment theory.

diagram.label: Combined and managed as a single whole

realWorldExample.description: Large pension funds around the world manage portfolios worth hundreds of billions of dollars, spread across stocks, bonds, real estate, and alternative assets - never concentrated in a single asset type.

quiz.question: Why should an investor think in terms of a portfolio rather than each investment individually?
options: Because a portfolio always returns more than any single stock
Because grouping them into one portfolio reduces the tax owed when taking profits
There's no special reason, it's just a tidier way to present holdings
Because the risk and return that matter belong to the portfolio as a whole
quiz.explanation: This is the foundation of Modern Portfolio Theory: an asset can be highly risky standing alone but actually REDUCE the portfolio's overall risk if it moves opposite to the other assets.

quiz.question: Is a portfolio holding only 2 stocks, both in banking, truly considered "diversified" just because it has 2 different assets?
options: Yes, having more than one asset already counts as diversified
Diversification only starts to matter from 10 assets and up
No - diversification needs low correlation, and two banks move together
Two or more assets is already enough to meet the diversification bar
quiz.explanation: The number of assets is not the sole factor determining real diversification - what matters more is the correlation between those assets.

quiz.question: How does a portfolio differ from a random basket of assets?
options: A portfolio is managed on the investor's behalf by a financial institution
A portfolio must contain at least ten different asset types
A portfolio only contains assets listed on a stock exchange
A portfolio has a purpose and weights chosen deliberately
quiz.explanation: Buying ten stocks because each ticker sounded good is ten individual investments, not a portfolio. A portfolio begins when weights are chosen to serve a predetermined goal and risk level.

quiz.question: Why does the weighting matter more than picking exactly the right assets?
options: Because the allocation across asset classes drives most of the variation
Because picking the right assets is something nobody can actually do
Because the weighting determines the annual trading fees owed
Because assets within the same class always deliver identical returns
quiz.explanation: Classic research shows the split between stocks, bonds, and cash explains most of a portfolio's variation over time. Picking a great ticker in 5% of the portfolio rarely offsets a bad allocation in the other 95%.

quiz.question: When should a portfolio be reassessed?
options: Every time the market drops more than five percent in a week
When the investor's goals or circumstances change
Daily, to stay on top of every single holding's movement
Only when a holding in the portfolio gets delisted
quiz.explanation: A portfolio serves a goal, not the news cycle. Having a child, changing jobs, or approaching retirement are legitimate reasons to rebalance; a single red week in the market is not.

keyTakeaways: Portfolio: a collection of assets managed as a single whole
Risk and return need to be assessed at the portfolio level, not for each individual asset
Portfolio thinking is the foundation of all of modern investment theory

practicePrompt.question: You hold 5 stocks, 2 bond funds, and a savings deposit. When assessing investment performance, should you look at each holding individually or at the whole picture? What concept describes this 'whole picture' approach?
options: You should only look at each investment individually, since each asset type has entirely independent risk-return characteristics
A portfolio is a collection of assets managed as a single whole, not the sum of separate holdings
This concept has no specific name in finance, it's just an ordinary perspective
You should sell off most assets to keep only one type, which is easier to track and assess
practicePrompt.explanation: Portfolio: a collection of assets managed as a single whole. Risk and return need to be assessed at the portfolio level, not for each individual asset - because how the assets correlate with each other has a major effect on overall risk.

application.title: List out your own portfolio
application.message: Write down everything you currently hold that has financial value - savings, stocks, gold, a life insurance policy with cash value - and look at them as a single unified portfolio instead of separate holdings.
application.secondary: Plenty of people have a portfolio they've never actually looked at as a whole.

sections.text: A portfolio is everything you hold - stocks, bonds, cash, gold, real estate - viewed as ONE unified block, not a pile of separate assets sitting next to each other. This is the single most important shift in thinking when an amateur investor becomes a serious capital manager: the question is no longer "is this stock good" but "what does this stock do for my portfolio".
Why look at the portfolio level?

A single asset can carry high risk standing alone, but when placed alongside other assets that move in the opposite direction, it can actually REDUCE the overall risk. This is exactly the foundation of Modern Portfolio Theory: the risk and return that genuinely matter belong to the whole portfolio, not to each individual investment. Judging each stock in isolation from the portfolio's context is the most common mistake new investors make.
Diversification is not just "holding many assets"

A portfolio holding only 2 bank stocks isn't necessarily truly diversified - both are exposed to almost the same forces from interest rates and industry regulation, so they tend to move together. The number of assets isn't what decides this; the correlation between them is what matters. A portfolio of 10 tech stocks can still be riskier than a portfolio of 3 assets from 3 completely different industries.

items: A portfolio covers every asset type you own, not just stocks
Assess risk/return at the whole-portfolio level, not for each individual holding
The number of assets isn't the same as quality of diversification - correlation is the key
This mindset is the foundation for every concept coming up in the Portfolio and Risk Management track: correlation, volatility, the Sharpe Ratio, MPT...

sections.label: A real-world example
sections.text: National pension funds manage hundreds of billions of dollars spread across stocks, bonds, real estate, and alternative assets - never dumping it all into a single asset type, however attractive that type might look.

lines: Before asking "should I buy this stock", ask "what will it do for my portfolio".
The portfolio is the correct unit of analysis - not each individual asset.
